notes.definition: The endocrine system is composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream. The blood carries each hormone to a target organ, where it produces an effect.
explanation: The endocrine system is the body's chemical coordination system. It is made up of glands, which secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Hormones are chemical messengers. Because the blood flows all around the body, a hormone reaches every organ, but it only produces an effect on its target organ (or organs).

Compared with the nervous system, the effects of the endocrine system are slower to start, because hormones have to be carried in the blood rather than as fast electrical impulses along neurones. However, hormonal effects act for longer. This makes hormones suitable for controlling long-term processes such as growth, puberty, the menstrual cycle and blood glucose concentration.

The pituitary gland, at the base of the brain, is called the "master gland". It secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions. These hormones in turn act on other glands, stimulating them to release other hormones that bring about effects. For example, follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary causes the ovaries to release oestrogen.

You need to be able to identify the position of the main glands on a diagram. The pituitary gland is at the base of the brain. The thyroid gland is in the neck. The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. The pancreas is in the abdomen, behind the stomach. The ovaries are in the lower abdomen of females, and the testes are in the scrotum of males.

Each gland produces particular hormones. The pancreas produces insulin, which helps control blood glucose. The ovaries produce oestrogen and the testes produce testosterone, the main reproductive hormones. The thyroid produces thyroxine and the adrenal glands produce adrenaline. You will study the roles of these hormones in more detail in later subtopics.
keyFacts: The endocrine system is composed of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
Hormones are chemicals carried by the blood to a target organ, where they produce an effect.
Hormonal effects are slower than nervous effects but act for longer.
The pituitary gland in the brain is the "master gland".
Pituitary hormones act on other glands, stimulating them to release other hormones.
Pituitary: base of brain. Thyroid: neck. Adrenal glands: on top of kidneys.
Pancreas: abdomen, behind the stomach. Ovaries: lower abdomen (females). Testes: scrotum (males).
Pancreas → insulin; ovaries → oestrogen; testes → testosterone; thyroid → thyroxine; adrenal glands → adrenaline.

keyTerms.definition: The system of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical secreted by a gland into the bloodstream, which carries it to a target organ where it produces an effect.
An organ that secretes (releases) chemicals such as hormones.
The organ on which a hormone produces its effect.
The "master gland" at the base of the brain, which secretes several hormones, some of which stimulate other glands to release hormones.
A gland in the neck that produces the hormone thyroxine.
Glands on top of the kidneys that produce the hormone adrenaline.

workedExamples.title: Comparing nervous and hormonal control
workedExamples.question: Response A starts 0.02 s after a stimulus and lasts 1 second. Response B starts 20 minutes after a stimulus and lasts several hours. Which is a hormonal response? Explain your answer.
steps: Recall that nervous responses are fast and short-lived because electrical impulses travel quickly along neurones.
Recall that hormonal responses are slower to start because hormones travel in the blood, but their effects last longer.
Response B is slow to start and long-lasting.
workedExamples.answer: Response B is hormonal: it is slower to start and acts for longer, which matches the endocrine system. Response A is nervous.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the master gland
workedExamples.question: The pituitary gland releases a hormone called TSH, which travels to the thyroid gland and causes it to release thyroxine. Use this example to explain why the pituitary is called the "master gland".
steps: The pituitary secretes a hormone (TSH) into the blood.
The blood carries TSH to another gland, the thyroid, which is its target organ.
TSH stimulates the thyroid to release its own hormone, thyroxine.
So the pituitary controls the release of hormones from other glands.
workedExamples.answer: The pituitary releases hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to release their hormones, so it controls much of the endocrine system.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hormones travel along nerves.
misconceptions.right: In fact hormones are carried in the bloodstream.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hormones only travel to their target organ.
misconceptions.right: In fact the blood carries hormones all around the body, but they only produce an effect on their target organs.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hormonal responses are faster than nervous responses.
misconceptions.right: In fact hormonal responses are slower to start but act for longer.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the pituitary gland controls every process in the body directly.
misconceptions.right: In fact the pituitary secretes hormones, several of which stimulate other glands to release their own hormones.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often put the adrenal glands in the brain or neck.
misconceptions.right: In fact the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys. The thyroid is in the neck.

realWorld: People with type 1 diabetes inject insulin because their pancreas does not produce enough of this hormone.
Children who do not produce enough growth hormone from the pituitary gland can be treated with growth hormone injections.
Blood tests for hormones such as thyroxine are used to diagnose thyroid problems, which can make people feel very tired or restless.
Hormones are used in contraceptive pills and fertility treatments to control the menstrual cycle.
examTips: Learn the AQA definition: glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
When comparing with the nervous system, give both parts: hormonal effects are slower AND act for longer.
Practise labelling the six glands: pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, ovaries and testes.
To explain "master gland", say the pituitary hormones act on other glands to stimulate the release of other hormones.
Use "secrete" and "target organ" in your answers; these are key words in mark schemes.
summary: The endocrine system is made of glands that secrete hormones into the blood.
Blood carries hormones to target organs, where they produce an effect.
Hormonal effects are slower than nervous effects but last longer.
The pituitary is the master gland: its hormones stimulate other glands.
Know the positions of the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries and testes.

questions.question: How do the effects of the endocrine system compare with those of the nervous system?
options: Faster and act for a shorter time
Slower and act for a shorter time
markScheme: 1 mark: slower but act for longer
questions.explanation: Hormones travel in the blood, so effects take longer to start, but they last longer than nervous responses.

questions.question: What is a target organ?
options: The organ where a hormone produces an effect
The organ that produces a hormone
The organ that removes hormones from the blood
markScheme: 1 mark: the organ where a hormone produces an effect
questions.explanation: Glands produce hormones; the target organ is where the hormone has its effect.

questions.question: Which endocrine glands are found only in males?
markScheme: 1 mark: testes
questions.explanation: Testes are only in males. Ovaries are only in females. Both sexes have adrenal and thyroid glands.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why the pituitary gland is called the master gland?
options: It is the largest gland in the body
It is the only gland connected to the brain by neurones
It secretes hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to release other hormones
It produces all of the hormones in the body
markScheme: 1 mark: its hormones stimulate other glands to release hormones
questions.explanation: The pituitary controls other glands through its hormones. It is not the largest gland and does not make all hormones.

questions.question: Which of these processes is most likely to be controlled by the endocrine system rather than the nervous system?
options: Growth of the body during puberty
Blinking when dust enters your eye
Pulling your hand away from a hot object
markScheme: 1 mark: growth during puberty
questions.explanation: Puberty is a slow, long-lasting process, which suits hormonal control. The other examples need very fast responses, which is the job of the nervous system.

questions.question: How do endocrine glands release their hormones?
options: Into the gut through a tube
Onto the surface of the skin
markScheme: 1 mark: directly into the bloodstream
questions.explanation: The AQA definition states that glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.

options: At the base of the brain
In the chest, next to the heart
markScheme: 1 mark: at the base of the brain
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is a small gland at the base of the brain.

questions.question: Name two glands that are part of the human endocrine system.
markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: pituitary; thyroid; adrenal gland; pancreas; ovaries; testes
questions.explanation: AQA requires you to know these six glands and their positions.

questions.question: What is the endocrine system composed of?
markScheme: 1 mark: glands (which secrete hormones into the blood)
questions.explanation: The endocrine system is composed of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.

questions.question: Describe how a hormone reaches its target organ.
markScheme: 1 mark: the hormone is secreted by a gland directly into the bloodstream
1 mark: the blood carries the hormone (around the body) to the target organ
questions.explanation: Hormones are carried by the blood. They reach all organs but only affect their target organs.

questions.question: Give two differences between the way the nervous system and the endocrine system send information.
markScheme: 1 mark: nervous system uses electrical impulses (along neurones); endocrine system uses hormones / chemicals (in the blood)
1 mark: nervous effects are faster / short-lived; hormonal effects are slower but act for longer
questions.explanation: Both systems coordinate the body but use different signals and work at different speeds.

questions.question: Explain why the pituitary gland is described as the master gland.
acceptedAnswers: stimulate other glands to release hormones
markScheme: 1 mark: it secretes (several) hormones into the blood (in response to body conditions)
1 mark: these hormones act on other glands, stimulating them to release other hormones
questions.explanation: The pituitary controls other glands through the hormones it releases.

questions.question: Name the glands that produce oestrogen.
markScheme: 1 mark: ovaries
questions.explanation: Oestrogen is the main female reproductive hormone, produced by the ovaries.

questions.question: Suggest why hormones, rather than nerves, are used to control processes such as growth and the menstrual cycle.
acceptedAnswers: carried in blood all around body
markScheme: 1 mark: these processes happen over a long time / need long-lasting effects
1 mark: hormonal effects act for longer / hormones in the blood can reach many organs; speed is not needed
questions.explanation: Hormonal effects are slower but long-lasting, which suits processes that take days, months or years.

questions.question: Suggest why damage to the pituitary gland could affect the functions of several other glands.
acceptedAnswers: other glands would not release hormones
markScheme: 1 mark: the pituitary secretes hormones that stimulate other glands
1 mark: so if it is damaged, other glands may not release their hormones / their target organs would not be affected
questions.explanation: Because the pituitary is the master gland, a problem there can disrupt hormones from glands such as the ovaries, testes or thyroid.

questions.question:
A hormone is injected into a muscle in the arm.
Explain how the hormone can affect an organ in the abdomen.
markScheme: 1 mark: the hormone enters the bloodstream
1 mark: the blood carries it around the body to the target organ in the abdomen, where it produces an effect
questions.explanation: Hormones travel in the blood, so they can reach target organs far from where they enter the body.

questions.question: Explain why a hormonal response takes longer to start than a nervous response.
markScheme: 1 mark: hormones are carried in the blood (which takes time to reach the target organ)
1 mark: nervous responses use electrical impulses that travel very quickly along neurones
questions.explanation: The blood carries hormones much more slowly than electrical impulses travel along neurones.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how one hormone from the pituitary gland affects the ovaries.
Use Figure 1 to explain the role of the pituitary gland in the endocrine system.

markScheme: 1 mark: the pituitary secretes FSH into the blood, which acts on another gland (the ovaries)
1 mark: this stimulates the ovaries to release a different hormone (oestrogen), so the pituitary controls other glands / is the master gland
questions.explanation: This example shows the pituitary working as the master gland: its hormone causes a second gland to release its own hormone.

questions.question: Describe the human endocrine system and how it coordinates responses in the body.
markScheme: Indicative content: composed of glands; glands secrete hormones; hormones are chemicals; released directly into the bloodstream; blood carries hormones to target organs; hormones produce an effect on the target organ; effects slower than nervous system but act for longer; pituitary gland is the master gland; pituitary hormones stimulate other glands to release hormones; examples of glands and positions: pituitary (base of brain), thyroid (neck), adrenal (on kidneys), pancreas (behind stomach), ovaries, testes.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of glands secreting hormones into the blood to target organs, with at least one further detail such as the master gland role or examples of glands.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as "glands make hormones" with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A strong answer gives the full sequence (gland, hormone, blood, target organ, effect) and adds detail about the pituitary or named glands.

questions.question: Compare the nervous system and the endocrine system as ways of coordinating the human body.
markScheme: Indicative content: both coordinate responses to changes / help maintain homeostasis; both involve detection of changes and effectors / target organs; nervous system uses electrical impulses along neurones; endocrine system uses hormones (chemicals) secreted by glands; hormones carried in the blood; nervous responses are very fast; hormonal responses are slower to start; nervous effects are short-lived; hormonal effects act for longer; nervous responses act on a precise area (specific muscle or gland); hormones travel all round the body but only affect target organs, and can affect several organs; nervous examples: reflexes; hormonal examples: control of blood glucose, growth, menstrual cycle; pituitary gland as master gland; the two systems can work together (for example glands are effectors in the nervous system).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed comparison with clear similarities and differences (signal type, transport, speed, duration, area affected) and suitable examples.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several differences described with some comparison; similarities may be missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one system or one difference.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Compare means giving similarities and differences side by side, for example "nervous responses are faster, whereas hormonal responses are slower but last longer".
